chib-068.title: Megadroughts grip tropical Africa
chib-068.text:
Drought drove early humans out of the heartland. From 135,000 years ago, megadroughts struck tropical Africa, pushing people toward the coasts and onto other continents. By the MIS 5 megadrought, 130,000 years ago, Africa held two ancestral human population clusters, including mtDNA haplogroup L0 in the south. Homo sapiens seems to have reached the western Sahelian zone by then.

Early modern human expansion in sub-Saharan Africa appears to have contributed to the end of late Acheulean (Fauresmith) industries about 130,000 years ago.

chib-071.title: Burials at Krapina
chib-071.text: Burials at Krapina, Croatia, date to about 130,000 years ago. Some anthropologists see in such burials a developing belief in an afterlife and a concern for the dead. Burial and ritual are among the religious behaviors people began to show in the Middle or Upper Paleolithic, alongside art. Some scientists propose that Middle Paleolithic societies such as the Neanderthals may also have practiced the earliest totemism or animal worship.

late-025.title: Bone harpoons at Katanda
late-025.text: Humans started fishing with barbed bone points. Bone harpoons from Katanda, in the Semliki River valley of Central Africa, date to about 90,000 years ago, in the Middle Stone Age. Harpoons were first invented in the late Middle Paleolithic, bringing fish into human diets as a hedge against starvation. The first evidence of fishing is also noted from artifacts at places such as Blombos Cave in South Africa. In Africa, bone artifacts and the first art appear in the same record.

late-063.title: Walking to Tasmania
late-063.text: Low glacial seas exposed a land bridge, and people walked across it. Aboriginal Tasmanians arrived about 40,000 years ago across the Bassian Plain. The bridge formed about 43,000 years ago; Tasmania's megafauna disappeared about 41,000 years ago, apparently through hunting. Australian megafauna extinction appears to have peaked around 42,000 years ago, earlier than in the Americas or among the Eurasian mammoth steppe fauna. The giant kangaroo Protemnodon died out sooner on the mainland than on Tasmania, which humans colonised a few thousand years later.

late-113.title: Rising seas flood the Persian Gulf
late-113.text: Rising seas from the melting ice sheets began flooding the Persian Gulf basin about 15,000 years ago. Much of the Gulf floor was still dry 12,000–9,000 years ago, and the modern marine Gulf formed in the early Holocene, by about 6,000 years ago. The Gulf is a foreland basin between the Arabian Peninsula and the Zagros Mountains of Iran.

late-123.title: The Great Lakes basins begin to fill
late-123.text: The Great Lakes are young water in an ancient hollow. They began forming around 14,000 years ago, as retreating ice sheets exposed the basins they had carved and meltwater filled them. In Wisconsin the ice also began to retreat then as the climate warmed. The meltwater lakes included Lake Algonquin, Lake Chicago, Glacial Lake Iroquois and the Champlain Sea. The foundations of the present upper Great Lakes were laid far earlier, 1.1 to 1.2 billion years ago, when two previously fused tectonic plates split apart and created the Midcontinent Rift.

gree-017.title: South America's last notoungulates die out
gree-017.text: South America's native hoofed mammals ended with the Pleistocene. Notoungulata lived from about 61 million to 11,000 years ago and included Toxodon, a rhinoceros-sized grazer. Their diversity declined during the Pliocene and Pleistocene, at the same time as the Great American Interchange let ungulates and other mammals from North America enter South America. Only the large toxodontids persisted until the end of the Pleistocene, and they perished in the Late Pleistocene megafauna extinctions along with most other large mammals across the Americas. Some Toxodon remains at Itapipoca, Brazil, and a tooth from another site gave even younger dates.

gree-033.title: The modern coyote appears
gree-033.text: The modern coyote appeared around 10,000 years ago, most likely descended from the Pleistocene coyote. The species itself is much older: by the Early Pleistocene, 1 million years ago, Canis latrans was already in existence.

gree-044.title: Today's Great Barrier Reef starts to grow
gree-044.text: The reef we see today is a latecomer on an old foundation. The present living Great Barrier Reef is believed to have begun growing on an older platform about 9,000 years ago. The land under it was a coastal plain formed from eroded sediments of the Great Dividing Range, with some larger hills that were mostly remnants of older reefs or, rarely, volcanoes. The reef system is the world's largest, made of over 2,900 individual reefs and 900 islands stretching over 2,300 kilometres across about 344,400 square kilometres.

nort-009.title: The last steppe bison
nort-009.text: The steppe bison outlived the mammoth steppe it grazed. It survived in north-central eastern Siberia until about 8,000 years ago, and bison DNA in northeastern Siberian permafrost may extend its survival to 5050–3800 BCE. A frozen mummy from northern Yakutia shows a pasture grazer living in a habitat becoming dominated by shrub and tundra vegetation. Bison in Alaska and the Yukon survived the loss of the mammoth steppe; the youngest North American remains, from Yukon, date to 3628–3377 BCE.

nort-010.title: Menengai collapses in Kenya's Rift Valley
nort-010.text: Menengai, a shield volcano on the floor of Kenya's Rift Valley, collapsed to form its 12 × 8 km caldera. The eruption is listed at VEI 6, with about 70 km³ of material. The volcano sits in the Great Rift Valley, part of an intra-continental system of depressions running north to south through Kenya.

nort-019.title: The Ilumetsa craters in Estonia
nort-019.text: Two probable meteorite craters, about 80 m and 50 m wide, formed together in southeastern Estonia. No meteorite fragments or shock features have been found, so the impact origin is probable rather than proven. That caution is fair, because some geological processes make circular or near-circular features that can be mistaken for impact craters.

nort-025.title: Pinatubo's Crow Valley eruptions
nort-025.text: Mount Pinatubo's Crow Valley eruptive period produced pyroclastic flows two to three times larger than those of 1991. The eruption is listed at VEI 6, with about 12 km³ of material. Later eruptions of modern Pinatubo came in episodes much shorter than the quiet intervals between them. The maximum size of eruptions in each period has been getting smaller over its 35,000-year history, though this might be an artifact of older deposits being eroded and buried.

nort-032.title: Mount Rainier collapses into the Osceola Mudflow
nort-032.text: About 5,000 years ago a huge part of Mount Rainier slid away, taking about 490 m off its summit. A sector collapse is the catastrophic failure of a significant part of a volcano, creating a large debris avalanche. This one fed the Osceola Mudflow, which reached the sites of today's Tacoma and south Seattle. Rainier has had large debris avalanches and enormous lahars, owing to the large amount of glacial ice on it.

nort-033.title: Burckle crater: a disputed impact
nort-033.text: A 29 km undersea feature in the southwest Indian Ocean may be a crater only about 5,000 years old, but other geologists dispute that it is an impact crater at all. The Holocene Impact Working Group proposes the impact, and its backers link it to floods that affected Sumerian civilization. A structure must meet a stringent set of established criteria to be confirmed. Proposing that Burckle (30 km) formed within the last few millennia has met with skepticism, since almost all confirmed craters younger than a million years are under two km across.

megh-014.title: The Caribbean's last ground sloths
megh-014.text: The last ground sloths lived on islands. Caribbean ground sloths on Cuba, Hispaniola and Puerto Rico lived possibly until 1550 BCE. Mainland ground sloths had died out about 11,000 years ago; the island relicts outlived them, much as Wrangel Island's mammoths did. They survived about 6,000 years longer, matching the fact that those islands were not colonized by humans until about 5500 yr BP. Ground sloths ranged from under 100 kilograms in the Caribbean to 3,700–4,100 kilograms in the largest genera Megatherium, Lestodon and Eremotherium.

megh-015.title: Did the last litopterns live into the late Holocene?
megh-015.text: Litopterns, an order of South American native hoofed mammals that arose 62.5 million years ago, are usually thought to have vanished about 12,000 years ago. A 2025 study of a Xenorhinotherium specimen radiocarbon dated to 3,493–4,217 years ago suggests the order survived into the late Holocene, though that rests on a single date. The last genera were Macrauchenia, Xenorhinotherium and Neolicaphrium. The order had nine families, of which Proterotheriidae and Macraucheniidae were the most diverse and the last to survive.

megh-020.title: Pinatubo's Maraunot eruption
megh-020.text: Mount Pinatubo in Luzon erupted at VEI 6 around 1050 BCE, ejecting about 12.5 km³ during its Maraunot eruptive period. It is an active stratovolcano in the Zambales Mountains in the Philippines. Its oldest eruption, Inararo, was also its largest.

megh-025.title: Raoul Island blasts open the Denham caldera
megh-025.text: About 2,200 years ago a major dacitic explosion on Raoul Island, in the Kermadecs, formed the 6.5 by 4 km Denham caldera. Rated VEI 6 and about the size of Krakatoa's 1883 eruption, it left the Fleetwood tephra; at one spot 40 m of pumice lies under 80 m of ignimbrite. The caldera's long axis runs parallel to the tectonic fabric of the Havre Trough, west of the volcanic arc. Historical eruptions in the 19th and 20th centuries were small-to-moderate phreatic ones, and some formed ephemeral islands in the caldera.

megh-027.title: Lake Chad's Bodélé basin dries out
megh-027.text: Lake Chad was once the largest lake on Earth. As Lake Megachad it grew to at least ten times its present size, then shrank to about 5% of its former size. Its deep northern Bodélé basin dried out completely about 2,000–1,000 years ago, cut off from the Chari River. The dry basin is today the largest single source of dust on Earth. Some studies suggest it supplies over half of the nutrient-rich dust that supports the Amazon rainforest.

megh-032.title: Ksudach's caldera-forming eruption
megh-032.text: Kamchatka's Ksudach volcano had a major caldera-forming eruption around 240 CE, ejecting 18–19 km³ and creating the 4 by 6.5 km Caldera V. The eruption is rated VEI 6. Ksudach has had five known collapse events, which created its system of nested calderas. Two lakes, Bolshoe and Kraternoe, lie within calderas at its summit.

megh-037.title: Mount Churchill spreads the White River Ash
megh-037.text: An Alaskan eruption rerouted trade across north-western Canada. Mount Churchill erupted at VEI 6 around 847 CE, ejecting about 50 km³ and laying the eastern lobe of the White River Ash. An earlier VEI 6 eruption about 145–345 CE laid the northern lobe. The eastern lobe is 2.5 centimetres thick 600 kilometres from the volcano and extends to the Great Slave and Great Bear Lakes. Archaeological data show some important trade routes were abandoned and new ones set up afterward, implying displaced people built new trade networks.

megh-059.title: The last wild aurochs dies in Poland
megh-059.text: The aurochs, wild ancestor of most modern cattle, once ranged across Eurasia, North Africa and India; only the European form survived into historical times. Hunting, forest clearance, competition with livestock and cattle diseases left one herd in Poland's Jaktorów forest. The last widely accepted aurochs cow there died of natural causes in 1627. Subfossil finds suggest wild aurochs may have survived in northwestern Transylvania until the 14th to 16th century and in western Moldavia until probably the early 17th century.

megh-066.title: The Great Lisbon earthquake
megh-066.text: On 1 November 1755 the Great Lisbon earthquake struck, one of the most destructive in history, killing around 100,000 people. It heads the list of large earthquakes and tsunamis the Azores–Gibraltar fault zone has produced since records began in the 1700s. That transform zone activated at about 30 Ma, appears as a ridge on the Atlantic Ocean floor, and is still an earthquake zone today.

megh-067.title: Steller's sea cow: gone in 27 years
megh-067.text: Steller's sea cow lasted only 27 years after its discovery. The largest known sirenian, at up to 10 m and 5–10 tonnes, survived as a relict in the Bering Sea's Commander Islands. Discovered in 1741, it was hunted for meat and hides until it was gone by 1768. In 1887 Stejneger estimated that fewer than 1,500 remained when Steller found them, and argued extinction was already an immediate danger. One study argues it was already a dead clade walking, since natural climatic and sea level shifts had wiped out most of the population and the tiny remainder risked a genetic extinction vortex.

megh-073.title: The 1831 eruption traced to Zavaritski Caldera
megh-073.text: A volcano nobody saw may have caused famines on two continents. A high-magnitude explosive eruption in the northern summer of 1831 may have come from Zavaritski Caldera on Simushir, in the Kuril Islands. Tephra layers found with the 1831 sulphate peaks in ice chemically matched its most recent Plinian eruption, dated to the early 19th century. Its reconstructed radiative forcing matches Pinatubo's in 1991 and may explain cooling in 1831–1833, ending the volcanic cold spell of 1809–1831. The sulfur is thought to have cooled the Northern Hemisphere by 0.5–1.0 °C, coincided with shifts in the Indian and African monsoons, and preceded famines including the Guntur famine of 1832 in India and the Tenpō famine in Japan.

megh-080.title: Santa María erupts in Guatemala
megh-080.text: Nobody in Guatemala knew Santa María could erupt. In October 1902 its first recorded eruption, a VEI 6, ejected about 5.5 km³ of magma over two days. Because it had no recorded eruptions, local people did not recognise the earlier seismicity as a warning. Between 7,000 and 13,000 people died. It ranks with Novarupta (1912) and Pinatubo (1991) among the three largest eruptions of the 20th century. New eruptions began in 1922 with a lava dome complex extruded in the crater the 1902 eruption left.

megh-083.title: Martha, the last passenger pigeon
megh-083.text: The passenger pigeon, once perhaps 40% of all birds in North America, was destroyed by habitat loss and mass hunting for a meat industry. It was declared extinct in 1914 when Martha, the last known bird, died at the Cincinnati Zoo, 20 years after the species vanished from the wild. Environmental laws passed to protect it did little to improve its numbers. The deforestation was also worsened by the invasive chestnut blight, which greatly reduced American chestnut trees.

megh-084.title: The last thylacine dies in Hobart
megh-084.text: The thylacine, or Tasmanian tiger, a dog-like marsupial predator, survived only in Tasmania; the last confirmed wild one was killed in 1931. The last known thylacine died at Hobart Zoo on 7 September 1936, though a 2023 analysis of sightings suggests it lingered for decades. Naturalist David Fleay shot a 45 second black-and-white film of the zoo's presumed last thylacine in 1933. Since 1996 Australia has marked National Threatened Species Day on 7 September.

megh-086.title: Iron rains on Sikhote-Alin
megh-086.text: On 12 February 1947 an iron meteorite of over 23 tonnes fell in the Sikhote-Alin Mountains of the Soviet Far East. Eyewitnesses saw a bolide brighter than the sun come out of the north and descend at about 41 degrees. Its fragments scattered over about 1.3 km² and blasted craters up to 26 m across. Before entering the atmosphere the meteoroid is estimated to have had a mass of about 90 tonnes.

megh-114.title: The 2010 Chile earthquake
megh-114.text: A magnitude 8.8 earthquake struck central Chile on 27 February 2010. It was the largest to hit Chile since the magnitude 9.5 1960 Valdivia earthquake and the strongest worldwide since the 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake. It triggered a tsunami with waves up to 24.1 m that devastated several coastal towns in south-central Chile, with the worst damage at Constitución. Its waves set off seiches as far away as Louisiana, and the Caldera del Atuel and other volcanic centres subsided afterward.

megh-124.title: The 2025 Kamchatka earthquake
megh-124.text: In 2025 another giant megathrust earthquake, of magnitude 8.8, struck the Kamchatka coast. Kamchatka lies on the Okhotsk plate, and the Pacific plate subducts beneath it along the Kuril–Kamchatka Trench.
